Foreign Buyers Pull Back From U.S., but Canadian Snowbirds Widen Their Lead

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Foreign homebuyers retreated from the U.S.
  • Between July and September 2026, global house hunters accounted for 1.3% of traffic on Realtor.com®, down from 1.5% a year ago, according to the latest quarterly International Demand report released on Wednesday.
  • Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu attributes the broader slowdown to a combination of factors, including geopolitical uncertainty, shifting trade policies, and persistent inflation challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Foreign homebuyers retreated from the U.S. housing market this fall, driven by an exodus of European shoppers. This shift helped Canadians cement their dominance.

Between July and September 2026, global house hunters accounted for 1.3% of traffic on Realtor.com®, down from 1.5% a year ago, according to the latest quarterly International Demand report released on Wednesday.

Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu attributes the broader slowdown to a combination of factors, including geopolitical uncertainty, shifting trade policies, and persistent inflation challenges.

Yet against that downturn, Canada's share of demand has expanded, climbing to 35.9% of overall international traffic and reinforcing its hold on the top spot among foreign buyers.

This development marks a turnaround from a year ago, when Canadian interest in U.S. real estate dipped to 32.3% amid President Donald Trump's aggressive tariff policies, which defined the beginning of his second term in office.

Sun-soaked Florida remains the premier destination for Canadian snowbirds escaping freezing Northern winters, commanding nearly 29% of Canada's search traffic.

Meanwhile, Texas edged past California as the second-most popular market for Canadians, drawing 8.8% of traffic compared with the Golden State's 8.6%.

"I’m seeing continued interest from Canadian buyers in Southern California," Daniel Zakharia, an agent with Douglas Elliman Beverly Hills, tells Realtor.com. "While political and economic uncertainty prompted some Canadian homeowners to reconsider their U.S. real estate holdings in 2025, particularly in traditional snowbird markets such as Palm Springs, recent reporting following the November midterm elections suggests that some Canadians are reconsidering their decisions to sell or stay away.".

Zakharia, himself a Canadian transplant, notes that California’s climate, lifestyle, and global connectivity remain fundamental attractions for Canadian buyers, who are most often drawn to turnkey properties with minimal maintenance, added privacy, security, and resort-style amenities.

The third-quarter 2026 data also highlights Montana's growing appeal, with the mountain state drawing 2% of Canadian search demand, up from 1.3% in 2019.

By comparison, Montana accounted for just 1.2% of overall international traffic during the same period.

"My experience has been that, typically, the Canadian buyers buy in the northern sections of Montana, as it has greater proximity to the border," Chase Heiland, real estate broker with Keller Williams Montana Realty, tells Realtor.com.

Echoing Xu, Heiland maintains that economic uncertainty surrounding tariffs on imports, elevated consumer prices, and an unfavorable exchange rate for the Canadian dollar are keeping many prospective buyers on sidelines.

However, those who do buy are taking a long-term view.

Heiland recently helped Canadians moving to Bozeman, MT, for a job opportunity to purchase a home in the area.

Recent findings suggest that "We walked through the pros and cons of single-family homes versus townhomes versus condos," he recounts. "They opted for a single-family home to best preserve its value moving forward, as well as being a good long-term investment into Bozeman and Montana as a whole.".

Despite cooling international demand nationwide, Heiland notes that he has worked with more overseas buyers this year than at any other point in his career.

Industry observers note that "Montana and Bozeman are very much on the map in a way they weren't before," indicates the agent. "I've had clients not only from Canada this year, but [also] from Russia, Mexico, and Pakistan. They all gravitated toward single-family homes in the city center, with access to everything Bozeman offers and easy access to the area's recreation.".

At the metro level, Cape Coral, FL, retained its strong pull among Northern neighbors, with roughly 66% of its international traffic coming from Canada in the third quarter, up 8.9 percentage points from a year ago for the largest annual gain among major markets.

Known as "the Venice of America," Cape Coral boasts over 400 miles of canals, many of them with golf course access, along with dozens of parks and family attractions.

Naples, FL, saw 65.4% of its foreign traffic coming from Canada in the third quarter, followed by Phoenix (62.6%) and North Port, FL (61.4%).

While Canada's share of international demand has grown year over year, Europe's has declined.

Europeans accounted for just under a quarter (24.5%) of all international homebuyers this fall, the lowest level since 2019, according to the quarterly data.

U.K. house hunters made up 6.2% of foreign traffic, followed by Germany at 3.7%, both marking seven-year lows for the third quarter.

Sources indicate that "The decline coincides with weaker European travel to the U.S., suggesting that European interest in U.S. homes may be cooling alongside interest in visiting," says Xu.

However, Zakharia points out that international buyer behavior is not uniform, and that it is crucial to distinguish between discretionary second-home purchases and those driven by professional or business opportunities.

Industry observers note that "I’m presently in discussions with a prospective buyer from the United Kingdom who is an actress considering relocating to Los Angeles and acquiring property because she sees greater opportunities for career advancement within the entertainment industry," says the agent. "This illustrates how international buyer demand can vary considerably depending on a buyer’s profession, industry, and long-term objectives.

Among the Europeans still looking to scoop up properties stateside, a growing share focused on New York and Texas.

In the third quarter, New York drew 8.1% of European traffic, up from 6% in 2019, while Texas attracted 8%, up from 7.1%.

Smaller states also gained ground among Europeans, with Montana's share nearly doubling, from 0.5% in 2019 to 0.9% this year, and Tennessee’s rose from 1.7% to 2.0%.

"International real estate demand is not simply a function of economics or politics," adds Zakharia. "It is also a function of where individuals see the greatest opportunities to build their careers, businesses, and lifestyles.".

The third-quarter traffic slowdown aligns with the National Association of Realtors® 2025 International Transactions in U.S. Residential Real Estate report, which found that international buyers purchased 14% fewer homes in U.S. compared to the prior year.

"The decline in foreign homebuyer activity mirrors the decline in international visitors and tourists to the United States," mentioned NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. "Even a slightly weaker U.S. dollar over the past year, which provides more purchasing power for foreigners, did not induce more activity.".

In the NAR data covering a period from April 2025 to March 2026, Canadians led foreign buyers, accounting for 16% of international transactions.

Industry observers note that snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in Latest York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

Tech Report: Europe’s Solar Problem Is No Longer Solar

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The rules, grids, and investment framework around it are struggling to keep up.
  • SolarPower Europe’s September mid-year assessment describes a familiar contradiction: solar is contributing more to energy security and affordability, yet weakening policy support, grid constraints, and insufficient flexibility threaten continued growth.
  • In its September newsletter, the association reported that solar became Europe’s largest electricity source in June and estimated that it avoided more than €30 billion in gas imports for power generation over six months of the Middle East conflict.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Europe’s solar fleet is delivering. The rules, grids, and investment framework around it are struggling to keep up.

SolarPower Europe’s September mid-year assessment describes a familiar contradiction: solar is contributing more to energy security and affordability, yet weakening policy support, grid constraints, and insufficient flexibility threaten continued growth.

In its September newsletter, the association reported that solar became Europe’s largest electricity source in June and estimated that it avoided more than €30 billion in gas imports for power generation over six months of the Middle East conflict. At that point, it forecast a slight contraction in EU solar deployment in 2026.

In a recent development, europe’s ambition to become an electrostate is stuck in a State of Confusion and will remain unconvincing unless its rules and networks catch up. The challenge is no longer simply building solar. It is connecting it, using it, and making participation easier.

Ukraine’s September auctions illustrate the shift.

In a recent development, preliminary results revealed that a 50 MW solar auction attracted three bids totalling 38.99 MW. A separate 100 MW solar-plus-storage auction attracted 26 bids totalling 385.9 MW.

Sources indicate that the terms differed: price ceilings were €0.08/kWh for standalone solar and €0.12/kWh for solar-plus-storage. These were bids, not completed projects. The results demonstrate stronger participation in the hybrid auction—not proof that adding batteries is inherently more profitable.

In a recent development, physical projects show the transition too. A September report described Romania’s 918 MWh battery under construction and a separate 120 MWh system commissioned at Teiuș. Bulgaria’s Devnya solar plant expanded from 5 MWp to 65 MWp, adding 60 MW/165 MWh of storage.

It has been revealed that but batteries are only part of the equation. Schneider Electric Research Institute’s October system-cost analysis models 40,500 scenarios combining distributed solar and batteries with central generation and networks.

Under global-average cost assumptions, optimised scenarios put total electricity-system costs about 10% below the benchmark, rising to as much as 40% below under assumed 2030s technology costs. These are modelled outcomes, not forecasts of European household bills.

The lesson from this company-sponsored research is coordination: electrifying transport, heating, and industry can improve infrastructure utilisation alongside distributed generation.

Denmark is confronting another bottleneck: access to scarce connection capacity.

Industry observers note that denmark’s October connection-prioritisation reform replaces a simple first-come, first-served approach with categories reflecting societal functions, electrification, and other uses. Within categories, projects placing less strain on the grid can receive priority.

In a recent development, battery treatment matters. Standalone storage falls in category 3, below renewable generation and electrification in category 2. Qualifying co-located batteries can also fall in category 2.

Sources indicate that storage can increase connection requirements or improve an existing connection’s utilisation. Rules should recognise operation, not merely technology labels.

Europe needs transparent queues, credible project-readiness tests and connection arrangements that reward flexibility—not just faster permitting.

According to recent reports, roofs, station canopies, car parks, and noise barriers already occupy space for another purpose. Adding PV can reduce additional land take, although it does not make generation footprint-free.

Recent findings suggest that belgium’s Solar Tunnel demonstrates the principle. A 2011 announcement records 16,000 modules installed on a covered section of the Paris–Amsterdam railway near Antwerp, designed to generate 3.3 GWh annually for railway infrastructure and trains.

Industry observers note that at Uden in the Netherlands, bifacial PV forms part of an A50 motorway noise barrier. The EU LIFE project’s monitored results recorded 325.5 MWh over 18 months—approximately 220 MWh annually.

It has been revealed that the assessment also reports lower-than-expected generation and higher-than-anticipated capital costs. Multifunctional infrastructure is promising, not automatically cheaper. Engineering, procurement, and maintenance determine whether combined benefits justify the premium.

According to recent reports, the strongest projects preserve their original function while adding electricity: shade plus charging, noise protection plus generation, or water infrastructure plus power. They complement conventional rooftop and ground-mounted solar rather than replace them.

At the other end of the scale, plug-in solar challenges the assumption that participation requires an owned roof and a substantial installation budget.

Germany’s Federal Network Agency provides a simplified administrative route for qualifying systems, with module capacity up to 2,000 Wp and inverter output up to 800 VA.

It has been revealed that registration remains mandatory. Separate network-operator notification is waived under specified conditions, including the unpaid-export arrangement. These administrative thresholds do not override technical or installation-safety requirements.

Germany’s environment agency explains that qualifying devices within technical limits can be commissioned by non-specialists.

That matters because administrative and installation costs can be disproportionate for small systems. Balcony solar offers a route for people without access to a conventional rooftop installation, including some apartment residents.

It does not replace large-scale generation or remove mounting, electrical-safety, building-consent, and country-specific requirements. Its importance is accessibility: proportionate regulation makes small-scale participation possible.

Europe needs large projects, distributed generation, solar-equipped infrastructure, accessible household systems, batteries, and flexible demand.

Sources indicate that writing from Down Under, the parallel is clear. High rooftop-solar penetration is reshaping Australian daytime demand and electricity prices. The response is batteries, flexible demand, and market rules that reward them.

Sources indicate that the choice is not between ambition and practicality. Practical rules are how ambition becomes deployment.

Prof Ray Wills is a Perth-based energy futurist and director of Future Smart Strategies, and Adjunct Professor at The University of Western Australia, who writes on renewables, electrification, and the energy transition.

#145273. These Are The Non-Car Vehicles You've Crashed

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1563 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

These Are The Non-Car Vehicles You've Crashed

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that crashing a car is a nightmare of physics, emotion and bodily injury.
  • Unsurprisingly, the Honda ATC makes multiple appearances in the comments section.
  • Man, they really don't make them like these vehicles anymore, and thank god.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that crashing a car is a nightmare of physics, emotion and bodily injury. The seriousness of the forces involved rarely make for a funny story. Luckily, these stories are not that. Earlier this week we asked you what vehicles you've crashed that were not cars, and it's clear some of you had childhoods built on survivor bias. Well, I, for one, am glad you survived ditching mountain bikes off of mountains and crashing lawnmowers into houses. Not just because you're still alive but, most importantly, you're alive and contributing to Jalopnik. That's right, you're still here for a very good reason.

Unsurprisingly, the Honda ATC makes multiple appearances in the comments section. Those three-wheeled off-roading vehicles are up their with lawn darts in the damage they caused Gen Xers. They were eventually banned in the U.S. because of the carnage. But you don't need to buy a dangerous vehicle to make it dangerous. Other interesting entries: a gas grill, a horse and a homemade go-kart.

Man, they really don't make them like these vehicles anymore, and thank god.

Just remembered the weirdest thing I've crashed.

According to recent reports, my dad had some land in West Virginia. There was a tiny river there and it had some very mild rapids that were more of a ford than a rapids, because it was no more than a foot deep. My sister and I would inflate air mattresses and ride them down the "rapids" normally joined by a dog riding a surfboard that was just a piece of foam shaped like one. Most of the time, the dog made the rapids fine, while my sister and I would run into rocks and the like with the air mattresses. Normally after a week of running the rapids, the air mattresses would be completely ruined by running into branches and sharp rocks.

According to recent reports, growing up, dad got a riding lawnmower (Sears 10 hp). Dad morphed it into also being a snow plow with weights on the rear wheels, a homemade plow and a lever to lift and lower it. We had it for years and we took absolutely no care of it other than making sure it had oil before we cranked it up.

One day, it went missing. By this time, it was at peak jank, with a pull starter, blades that never stopped and an uneven deck that was set to dang near chopping up the roots of the grass. It didn't take Columbo to figure how where it was, as we traced a scalped path through many neighbors' lawns and to the river about 1/2 mile away, where the path of 5 O-clock shadow grass ended and the river began. Some drunk teenager discovered that the brake pedal was disconnected, but didn't discover the way to stop it was to drop it into low gear and turn off the engine.

Industry observers note that oh jeez, that's a list. Dirt bikes of all sizes, same with quads a trike or two, several flavours of boat including a canoe (that shoal jumped in front of me!) but probably the most memorable, or at least the most story worthy is the scooter my buddies dad rented for us when we went on a joint family vacation to Cancun back in the late 90s.

It has been revealed that he rented four, two for me and my friend, one for him and one for the older brother and we went ripping around Playa Langosta the way three teens and an adult that branded himself the 'fun' dad could. Getting progressively dumber and riskier as the afternoon wore on. Eventually as the rental time was running out we decided to make a race of it and I was confident enough after a few hours of pinning that little 50cc Honda that I figured I could lean it like a race bike around a corner.

I could not and luckily came away with it with minimal road rash and a big ol bruise on my shoulder.

According to recent reports, the scooter was not so lucky, nor was the magazine stand it slid into. Fortunately insurance had been purchased, unfortunately fun dad was not so fun the remaining days of the trip.

According to recent reports, I've had my share of mountain bike crashes. The most recent bad one was on a slightly downhill rock field (a bunch of bowling ball sized boulders packed into the trail for 60 feet as a technical feature).

I was going a little too fast, got off the proper line, and went down on my side. Normally this wouldn't be a big deal except rock fields are not very forgiving.

I cracked a couple of ribs which was problematic in that this trail didn't have any short cuts out so I had to ride another 8 miles or so in not very good condition as it was very painful to breathe.

I was sore for a couple months. I also learned to no longer judge NFL QBs who wear flack jackets to protect their ribs. Most painful injury I've ever had. You just have to gut it out.

Back in the '80's my uncle had a farm that I would go work/play on in the summer. My uncle and cousins had just gotten four ATC200 three wheelers that Spring and my cousins and I were all super excited to race 'em all over the farm that summer. I get up there right after school ends and immediately we're off riding through ditches, bombing across fields and having a blast. The big red barn on the farm was at the top of a steep hill with a gravel drive up to and around it. We'd practice to screaming up the gravel drive and as it leveled out, use the negative G-force to whip the tail out into a lurid slide/drift all the way around the barn. On the other side of the barn was the Milking House, so you'd carry the slide between the two buildings with the echo of the screaming 4 stroke bouncing off the walls. Gaining confidence in this technique, we would just continually elevate the speed. First getting air at the top of the hill, then starting the slide later and eventually clipping apexes and throwing gravel everywhere. This abruptly came to an end when I came up the hill the fastest I'd ever gone, got a late start in my slide, went way too wide and clipped the front corner of the milking house on the other side of the barn. The rear axle of the ATC snapped, throwing me over the bars into the side of the milking house and onto the gravel in a heap. This led to the saying in our family, "that boy couldn't hit the broad side of a barn, but sure can nail a milking house!".

In a recent development, I crashed a Honda ATC when I was maybe 11 or 12 years old. Going way too fast in a large horse pasture when I hit a large dip. Flipped me over, and I'm lucky it didn't land on me. Walked away with a black eye and some scrapes and bruises. 0/10 – do not recommend.

Gen X survivor checking in: if you haven't flipped or nearly paralyzed yourself with a Honda 3-wheeler ATC, you're not really one of us.

From Black Mac and cdoggyd and BuddyS and others (so many others).

According to recent reports, my dad built me a homemade go-kart with a 5-hp Briggs & Stratton engine. This was no professional shifter kart chassis. It's exactly what you envision when you think "homemade." Only the right rear wheel was powered. We would take it to the local elementary school on weekends because it had a really large asphalt playground out back and no gates. I'd rip laps for a while until I got tired and we'd go home.

It has been revealed that I always went clockwise around the lot. Then one day, I decided I wanted to turn left like my heroes in NASCAR. I got a nice lesson in centrifugal force with the powered wheel now on the inside. It pushed me wide and I hit the curb that separated the asphalt lot with the grass field. I did my best Tony Hawk impression as I did a curb grind for several feet on the floor of the cart. What really stood out to me later is that luckily it happened where it did and not the other side of the lot which would have submarined me under a metal bench face first.

There isn't anything that moves I probably haven't crashed. Motorcycles, boats, 4 wheelers, snowmobiles, sleds, coaster wagons, bicycles, wheelbarrows, gas grill, and more. Even hit the house with a lawn mower. I learned a zero steer mower sometimes has "zero" steer on wet grass.

It has been revealed that raleigh Chopper. Tore-off a toenail (riding true 1969 style – barefoot in bellbottoms) and broke a tooth. Good times!

Golf carts are my greatest fear in the world because I watched too many camp counselors drive them like demo derby cars. More than once I saw someone try to do a J-turn on one and roll it over and I was certain I just watched someone die.

  • According to the seller, the 454 V8 was rebuilt and received a replacement camshaft roughly 5,000 miles ago.
  • It has been revealed that the Fisher body tag demonstrates that the pickup was originally painted Placer Gold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're shopping for El Caminos, then this 1971 example should pique your interest. Listed on Bring a Trailer, the pickup has 47,000 miles on the odometer and features a 454 massive-block V8 paired with a four-speed manual transmission. The El Camino in question has been with the seller since 1992 and comes with the build sheet (albeit a tattered one) and a Nevada title.

According to the seller, the 454 V8 was rebuilt and received a replacement camshaft roughly 5,000 miles ago. BaT's description notes that the car's true mileage can't be verified, but that hasn't stopped potential buyers from placing their bids, with the highest bid sitting at $8,500 at the time of writing.

It has been revealed that the Fisher body tag demonstrates that the pickup was originally painted Placer Gold. The body, as you can see from the pictures, has since been refinished in red, with black striping on the hood. There are chrome details on the bed rails and wheel openings, as well as chrome bumpers and a drop-down tailgate. Locking pins secure a cowl-induction hood, which was added later. Completing the exterior are 14-inch Rally-style wheels fitted with derby-style hubcaps and wrapped in BFGoodrich white-letter tires.

It has been revealed that on the inside, the cabin has black vinyl seats with color-matched carpeting, door panels, and dashboard. And per the Fisher body tag (trim code 706), this El Camino appears to have left the factory with a black vinyl interior. Other highlights include power steering and brakes, a Muncie shifter, a center console, and a Pioneer cassette player.

Sources indicate that if you came across this listing earlier, you probably wondered why BaT hadn't listed the car with an SS 454 headline if it was the real deal. There was certainly a lot of activity in the comment section, with doubts surrounding the car's authenticity. Much of the discussion centered on documenting the drivetrain, with commenters coaching the seller on where to find the partial VIN stamped on the engine block.

The more knowledgeable commenters helped resolve the question after the seller posted photos of the VIN stamp on the block, the rear end, and the Posi tag. User ssterry commented, "Congratulations! Photos #129-131 should be more than adequate to convince BaT that this El Camino was born an SS!" BaT agreed, writing in a November 25 comment, "We've reviewed the additional media, and have updated the listing to reflect that the car is an El Camino SS 454.".

As you may know, the 454 found its way into a lot of Chevy trucks, including car-based utes like the El Camino. But unlike the more coveted 1970 LS6-equipped models, 1971 SS 454s used the LS5 version of the big-block V8. Even though the LS5 doesn't have the LS6's numbers, the 454 LS5 is still a fairly robust powerplant, rated at 365 gross horsepower and 465 pound-feet of torque (or 285 hp and 390 lb-ft SAE net) for the 1971 model year. Pair that with the four-speed stick, and you have yourself a brilliant excuse for skids and donuts.

The Nevada-based seller appears to be new to the platform. But the comments and the seller's interaction with them have really helped settle the SS question. Get in the mix and place a bid if you're interested. The auction ends on Saturday, November 28.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The company launches a competitive bidding process for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan solar energy.

DTE Energy has unveiled plans to add up to 150 megawatts of newly introduced solar energy in Michigan, creating construction jobs, supporting local communities, and saving customers money on fuel costs.

Because solar generation does not require fuel, the upcoming projects will help reduce the organization’s exposure to changing fuel prices over their operating lives. The projects will also support DTE’s work to provide customers with energy that is reliable, increasingly clean, and affordable.

Sources indicate that “These projects are an investment in Michigan and the communities we’re proud to serve. By producing more Michigan-made energy that doesn’t require us to purchase fuel, we can help lower energy costs for our customers and reduce our reliance on fuel from outside our state. At the same time, these projects will create good jobs and bring newly introduced investment and tax revenue into local communities, providing more resources for schools, first responders and the services Michigan families count on every day.”.

Sources indicate that DTE is seeking competitive proposals for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan-based solar generation. The procurement supports the requirements of the settlement agreement in Michigan Public Service Commission Case No. U-21662, approved May 15, 2025.

It has been revealed that projects must achieve commercial operation by June 30, 2030, be located in Michigan and connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE’s distribution system. Interested bidders can register and obtain additional information through PowerAdvocate. Proposals are due Jan. 19, 2027, and DTE expects to execute contracts in the second or third quarter of 2027.

Sources indicate that DTE is Michigan’s leading producer of and investor in renewable energy, generating enough clean energy from wind and solar to power nearly 1 million homes. As the company works toward net zero carbon emissions, it remains committed to growing its renewable energy portfolio while maintaining a balanced mix of energy resources that supports reliability and affordability for customers. DTE’s 2026 Integrated Resource Proposal builds on that commitment, calling for an additional 15 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2042.

Cigna is making $31.5 million in grant funding available over the next three years to nonprofits in 10 states that are aiming to tackle several key community health priorities.

The company said that funds will be made available through its philanthropic arm, the Cigna Group Foundation, with applications open now through Dec. 18. Cigna said in an announcement that it's looking for organizations tackling youth mental health, veteran wellness and the impact of complex health needs on patients and their caregivers.

Cigna stated the program seeks to deepen the tech giant's community health strategy to address critical challenges.

The company first introduced a newly introduced approach to community health and engagement in 2024, and since then has deployed more than $30 million in funding to 190 nonprofit organizations. Projects backed by these grants have reached at least 321,000 people, Cigna stated.

Sources indicate that "Over the past several years, we’ve seen the tangible impact we can make when we invest in strong nonprofit partners and come together to help communities achieve better health and vitality," said Melissa Skottegaard, board chair of The Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. "We’re building on what’s working, bringing together funding, collaboration and the skills of our employee volunteers to address some of the most pressing health challenges facing communities across the street and around the world.".

Cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. Youth mental health, for example, has been a leading topic at the company for some time, and the company said it will also continue to build on its partnership with the Boys and Girls Clubs of America in this area.

Recent findings suggest that in that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The tech giant mentioned that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

In a recent development, eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, Latest Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

Cigna remarked its foundation will also continue to support community health through its Health Equity Impact Fund.

Sources indicate that "Community organizations can be a powerful source of support for people navigating complex health conditions,” stated Matt Perlberg, president of Evernorth Pharmacy & Care Delivery and board member of the Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. “By helping patients and caregivers connect with resources and overcome barriers to care, these organizations can provide important support alongside essential medical treatment, helping people navigate their health and care journey.”.

The show has been through some fraught years recently, with dozens of presenters coming and going since the Clarkson/Hammond/May trio were forced to scarper off to Amazon's Grand Tour over a decade ago. He's famous, is what I'm saying.

"Top Gear" has been off the air since the most recent run with hosts Chris Harris, Freddie Flintoff, and Paddy McGuinness fizzled out in 2022. My personal favorite era was the 2018-2019 run, with Harris showing off his skills opposite Rory Reid and Matt LeBlanc. There's no word yet as to who will complete the on-screen personality roster with Ramsay, but he'll probably have pretty good chemistry with just about anybody they pick. The sixty-year-old star is getting on a bit in years, but he seems to be able to chop it up and chew the fat with just about anyone. He's been a charismatic and over-the-top TV guy for decades, and knows what makes a show interesting.

While filming begins next year, the show won't hit the airwaves until 2028, so we still have some time until we can see just what this guy has in store for us. Surely, it'll include some international travel, jovial competition, on-track action with The Stig, and stars in reasonably priced cars. Hopefully at least one of Ramsay's co-presenters is too young to receive a pension, eh?

"Top Gear" has had some pretty awful fits and starts over the last decade plus, as the BBC has tried to fit in some non-standard car show presenters. The worst of which was almost assuredly radio DJ and producer Chris Evans, who helmed the show in 2016 despite having severe motion sickness and knowing next to nothing about cars. Ramsay, to his credit, is a massive car fanatic. He follows F1 religiously, is frequently seen on the grid before races, and recently competed in the celebrity Lego karting race ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Gordon's collection includes millions of quid worth of Ferraris, McLarens, Porsches, Astons, Land Rovers, and more. Apparently he is frequently seen at Brands Hatch driving his BAC Mono track weapon, which certainly endears me to his sensibilities. He has said that his love of the Ferrari brand was inspired by the TV show Magnum P.I., and he has owned dozens of cars from the brand, including a pair of LaFerrari (coupe and Aperta), an SP2, an SP3, an 812 Superfast, an F12 Tour de France, and more.

Ramsay was a guest on the old Top Gear (when they still had the Cool Wall in the studio) during the first season of the show's original run, airing on December 22 of 2002, back when he was still in his 30s. He had some amusing anecdotes, especially about cooking with car engine. When he took the old Suzuki Liana out around the Dunsfold test track, he looked pretty darn competitive on a dry day. In the end he put down a 1-minute 50-second lap, which tied him with Jeremy Clarkson's best, and just a tick shy of Jay Kay's board leading spot.

Industry observers note that sound off in the comments with your thoughts on Ramsay as presenter, and who you think the BBC should pair with Ramsay for the best results. Are you excited about Top Gear's return? Do you think it'll stick around for a while with Gordon at the helm? I just hope it's good. There hasn't been any good car television lately!

Hybrids Are a Waypoint, Not the Destination

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1404 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An earlier version of this article appeared in The Driven on 15 October 2026.
  • Sources indicate that in January 2024, Toyota chairman Akio Toyoda said battery EVs would reach at most 30% market share, with the remainder going to hybrids, hydrogen, and combustion vehicles.
  • PHEVs are conditional transition vehicles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An earlier version of this article appeared in The Driven on 15 October 2026. This version has been revised and updated with the most recent registration data.

By Ray Wills, Raphael Wellmann, and Peter Newman.

Sources indicate that in January 2024, Toyota chairman Akio Toyoda said battery EVs would reach at most 30% market share, with the remainder going to hybrids, hydrogen, and combustion vehicles. Norway’s BEV share was already at about 89% that year. Norway alone cannot settle a prediction about the global market, but it shows that 30% is no inherent ceiling on BEV adoption.

PHEVs are conditional transition vehicles. They earn their environmental case through verified electric kilometres, not through the presence of a charging port.

It has been revealed that mature markets tell the more revealing story. Once battery-electric vehicles offer sufficient choice, charging confidence, and competitive economics, hybrids do not settle into a permanent share of the market. Hybrids may lead early, peak, and then retreat.

Norway. The year is 2015. Hybrid vehicles had gained material market share and plug-in hybrids were beginning to arrive in volume. In 2017, PHEVs accounted for about 18% of upcoming registrations. BEV growth temporarily paused, while hybrids benefited from familiar factories, familiar supply chains, and familiar consumer expectation.

It has been revealed that after another PHEV surge in 2020 and 2021, the direction changed. By October 2026, battery-electric vehicles accounted for 98.8% of Norway’s newly introduced passenger-car registrations. Petrol plug-in hybrids represented just 0.2%, and petrol full hybrids 0.3%. Across the first ten months of the year, BEVs held 98% of the market. Hybrids had not become a permanent destination: they had become marginal in new-car sales.

It would be easy to dismiss Norway as a special case: a small, affluent, and subsidy-supported market.

Singapore has a distinctive vehicle-ownership system, built around Certificates of Entitlement, high ownership costs, and tightly managed taxation. Yet its market also reveals hybrids losing ground as BEVs expand. Conventional hybrids accounted for 28.3% of new registrations in October 2026, while BEVs held 59.6% and PHEVs 6.2%. The monthly figures fluctuate: hybrid share was higher than in August. The longer-term question is whether hybrids retain their earlier prominence as BEVs become mainstream—not whether their share falls every month.

Sources indicate that denmark provides another example. In October 2026, battery-electric vehicles accounted for 88.2% of all newly introduced passenger-car registrations and 97.4% of households’ new cars. The distinction matters: household purchases and the overall market do not electrify at precisely the same pace. But both now show BEVs becoming the dominant choice.

Industry observers note that these three markets are not identical, and their policies are not interchangeable. But they show a repeating shape. In leading electrification markets, hybrid share has not settled into a stable plateau. It has risen, peaked and then declined.

That is what a waypoint looks like.

For years, Norway was treated as the exception: small, rich, subsidy-heavy, and unrepresentative. But its basic market pattern is now appearing wherever electrification has advanced far enough.

Once the pattern is visible in several unrelated countries, the question becomes whether it is appearing more widely, including in markets still early in the transition.

Trailing-twelve-month registration data across the selected markets show not a world divided between “BEV countries” and “hybrid countries,” but markets at different stages of electrification and following different routes.

In a recent development, some move relatively directly from combustion vehicles to BEVs. Others pass through a stronger hybrid phase, then a PHEV phase, before BEVs become dominant. In China, PHEVs and range-extended EVs have gained strength alongside BEVs, supported by rapid product cycles, intense domestic competition, expanding charging networks, regulatory settings, and strong domestic manufacturers.

This is not a claim that hybrids have already peaked everywhere. Across the European Union, BEVs accounted for 23.4% of fresh-car registrations in the first ten months of 2026, while hybrids remained a major part of the market. In Australia, the hybrid share is still close to its high, but in October 2026, BEVs overtook hybrids on a trailing-twelve-month basis for the first time (18.5% vs. 17.6%). The transition remains uneven across countries, buyer types, and vehicle segments.

Recent findings suggest that the route differs. The starting point differs. The pace differs. The picture that comes out isn’t “some countries like BEVs, others like hybrids.” As BEVs meet more buyers’ needs at competitive cost, hybrids face increasing pressure on their share of upcoming-car sales. Whether their absolute sales also fall depends on the size and growth of the market.

According to recent reports, there is a practical implication for buyers. A hybrid purchased today in a market that has not yet reached its tipping point may face greater residual-value risk when it arrives on the used market. If upcoming-car demand shifts rapidly towards BEVs while used supply reflects today’s hybrid-heavy sales, resale values may come under pressure.

Fuel prices, tax settings, used-BEV supply, charging access, and export markets will impact, but it is a risk buyers, fleets, and financiers should acknowledge.

If the pattern is visible in the data, why does public discussion so often present hybrids as a permanent pillar of the future vehicle market?

One reason is that the transition is uneven—the future is here, it’s just not well distributed yet. In many countries, people have only seen the rising half of the hybrid curve. The peak and decline have not yet arrived. It is easy to mistake “still growing” for “here to stay.”.

Recent findings suggest that another is that manufacturers with decades of investment in combustion and hybrid platforms have commercial reasons to extend the life of those systems. That behaviour seems rational. Hybrid platforms preserve familiar engines, suppliers, dealer servicing, and factory investments.

According to recent reports, but that commercial logic is not evidence that hybrid demand will remain durable once BEVs can do the same job more effectively. As with everything, the biggest cost may come not in going too fast, but in going too slow.

It is also important not to overstate the case against PHEVs. A PHEV that is routinely plugged in can cover much of its owner’s daily driving on electricity. The problem is that many of those PHEVs are not used that way.

In a recent development, european Commission data from 320,000 PHEVs first registered in 2021 found real-world CO₂ emissions averaging 3.5 times their official type-approval values. The Commission concluded that these vehicles were not being charged and driven electrically as frequently as assumed in laboratory testing.

Company vehicles are a particular problem. Petrol may be employer-paid, immediate, and simple to use, while home charging is paid by the employee, workplace charging is unavailable, and reimbursement is cumbersome. Under those conditions, the petrol engine becomes the default.

A PHEV is a bridge—but only if people use it to cross from the petrol side to the electricity side.

In a recent development, the registration data do not say that every hybrid buyer has made the wrong decision. Some households and fleets still need a transitional option. Some regional, towing, remote-area, and high-kilometre uses remain difficult for today’s BEV models and charging networks.

But those are specific use cases that are not representative of the mass market and thus not a reason to preserve combustion systems for everyone.

Recent findings suggest that conventional hybrids reduce petrol consumption, particularly in stop-start urban driving, but every kilometre still depends on fuel. PHEVs can replace a substantial share of petrol with electricity, but only if they are regularly charged, have enough real-world electric range, and do not unnecessarily run their engine.

BEVs eliminate routine petrol use and are the most energy-efficient option for the expanding share of households and fleets whose driving and charging conditions suit them.

It has been revealed that the role of policy is not to pretend that all drivers are identical. It is to make electric driving easier: reliable charging at homes, apartments, workplaces, and regional routes; electricity reimbursement as straightforward as fuel reimbursement; and real-world reporting of petrol use and electric kilometres in PHEV fleets.

The market is not likely to move from combustion to BEV in exactly the same way everywhere. But as battery-electric vehicles become cheaper, more capable, and easier to charge, the addressable market for hybrids contracts.

Hybrids can help drivers transition from the combustion era into the battery electric era.

But that is all they are, a waypoint towards an electric future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Elsevier unveiled this week a major upgrade to ClinicalKey AI, enabling the AI-powered clinical decision support tool to access a patient’s full electronic health record and evaluate treatment plans against the company’s evidence-based medical library.

As AI advances, Elsevier has strategically shifted from a traditional academic publisher—it’s one of the world's largest publishers of scientific, technical and medical content—to an AI-driven analytics information organization, incorporating generative and agentic AI into its healthcare and academic research.

Industry observers note that clinicalKey AI is a HIPAA-ready point-of-care decision support tool that draws answers from articles sourced from approximately 1,000 world-leading journals. Elsevier’s upgraded ClinicalKey AI is already deployed at more than 1,200 hospitals, and the tech giant indicates the solution integrates with all EHR providers. Elsevier recently struck a content agreement with the JAMA Network that brings full-text content and visuals from the JAMA Network Family of Journals to ClinicalKey AI.

ClinicalKey AI was originally co-developed through a strategic partnership between Elsevier and OpenEvidence. An Elsevier spokesperson stated the company's collaboration with OpenEvidence on ClinicalKey AI has concluded.

Sources indicate that the tech giant has rapidly expanded its AI capabilities and features, including ClinicalKey Nursing AI, an AI-powered tool built specifically for nurses and nursing workflows. Elsevier has also developed specialized AI assistants, such as LeapSpace, an AI-assisted workspace for researchers that’s built on 15+ million peer-reviewed articles and book content and 100 million Scopus records, according to the company.

It has been revealed that three months ago, the tech giant rolled out its "Ask AI" feature across more than 1,500 U.S. hospital sites using its flagship ClinicalKey platform. With the generative AI feature, clinicians can ask conversational clinical questions and receive direct, cited answers drawn from evidence-based sources, including premium journals and content from leading medical organizations, the company noted. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, Ask AI does not pull from the open web and does not store, process or retain patient-identifiable information, according to the company.

It has been revealed that in a move to develop context-aware AI, the firm acquired Wellsheet in June. The health technology company aggregates and synthesizes patient chart data—including notes, labs, imaging and medication orders—from EHRs to provide relevant clinical intelligence at the bedside.

Recent findings suggest that “The problem we’re trying to solve here is that physicians are challenged by so many things when they’re taking care of patients; top among them is patient complexity. Patients have more and more conditions, and they’re taking more and more medications. It can be hard to really understand the full picture and determine how to proceed,” Dr. Claudine Lott, physician executive for clinical solutions at Elsevier, told Fierce Healthcare during the HLTH conference this week.

“Our original ClinicalKey AI tool has been a place where the clinician can go, and they can ask a question, and it searches this curated database of evidence-based content we’ve given it and gives them an answer. But there was a bit of a missing piece in that it wasn’t capturing that patient context. If you wanted to get an answer, that’s really tailored to a patient, it was limited to what you can type in,” she said.

She added, “Wellsheet has 10 years of experience with looking at the entirety of the patient chart and helping to surface that to the clinician.”.

There is a growing market for AI-powered clinical decision support products, but Elsevier contends its advantage lies in its depth of patient context and its large, curated content base, with a wholly owned, large proprietary library of peer-reviewed STM literature, including content from millions of articles, journals and books.

San Juan Regional Medical Center in Farmington, Latest Mexico, is using ClinicalKey AI’s new patient context functionality to provide quality care with fewer resources. With smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic health systems, and in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid, the medical center, which serves the Four Corners area, has found this support especially valuable, according to Carlo Hallak, M.D., physician executive, information services, at San Juan Regional Medical Center.

A non-profit, community-owned acute care hospital and Level III trauma center, San Juan Regional Medical Center operates outpatient and specialty clinics alongside its main hospital campus, San Juan Regional Rehabilitation Hospital and San Juan Health Partners clinics.

Hallak emphasized that Elsevier is a primary source of medical knowledge rather than a “wrapper” for other AI platforms, and that was a key distinction for the organization, he noted. And ClinicalKey AI is designed for the entire care team. “The hospital is run by nurses, mid-level providers, other caregiver teams,” he told Fierce Healthcare at the HLTH conference.

The medical center aims to move clinicians to enterprise LLMs integrated with the electronic health record that can provide the full patient context, Hallak noted.

"We're already seeing how ClinicalKey AI can be instrumental at the bedside and help improve care for our patients. As a rural healthcare center, we are proud to say that by using ClinicalKey AI to check each patient’s care against the same evidence base that major health systems rely on, we’re able to deliver the standard of care patients expect in any major city or leading academic center," Hallak mentioned.

He added, "ClinicalKey AI reads the whole chart, checks it against the evidence and indicates exactly where each finding comes from. That support is invaluable for a hospital like ours, and we’re already seeing strong adoption of ClinicalKey AI among our clinicians.".

Hallak cited an example of a physician who used ClinicalKey AI to correctly identify viral meningitis, preventing an aggressive and unnecessary treatment course for bacterial meningitis.

According to recent reports, clinicalKey AI supports the physician’s judgment rather than replacing it, helping the clinician get to relevant evidence faster, he said, noting that, in the case of the viral meningitis patient, the physician’s clinical judgment was critical in recognizing that something was unusual and then consulting colleagues. The AI tool then helped accelerate the next step by quickly surfacing information the clinician otherwise would have found by searching the medical literature.

Physicians also use the tool during weekly complex case discussions to quickly review trending medications, images and test results in one summarized sheet, he noted.

“It’s going to expedite a lot of the work they do when it comes to these complex cases,” he said.

The AI solution can rapidly summarize a complex patient history at the point of care, and this can help care teams in the emergency department understand a frequent ED patient, Hallak said.

One patient has visited their emergency department 95 times in less than a year, in addition to making numerous visits to neighboring health systems, Hallak remarked. When that patient arrives, clinicians who aren't familiar with him would traditionally have to dig through the chart to understand his history. With Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI tool, they can ask for a summary of the patient's recent visits and care and get that information within seconds, he noted.

Because patients who frequently visit hospital EDs typically receive care at multiple organizations, San Juan Regional Medical Center is also working with other local health systems on interoperability efforts so clinicians can get a more complete picture of what happened during the patient's visits across different facilities.

As a rural hospital with staffing constraints, technology is essential to filling workforce gaps and supporting care delivery, Hallak contends.

According to recent reports, "We don't have enough physicians, enough nurses, enough transporters, enough caregivers. We will never be able to have enough of those," he remarked.

Hallak envisions ClinicalKey AI will be particularly valuable for discharging patients from the hospital faster.

According to recent reports, generative AI tools can help speed up patient discharges by identifying barriers, assessing patients’ care needs and providing relevant information from both structured and unstructured data. Because the platform is designed for the broader care team, case managers and physicians can access the same information, while push notifications can alert clinicians when test results are available so they can act rapidly, Hallak said.

"From an operational perspective, it allows for this care team coordination of care, and also from a physician perspective, it provides the context whenever there's something hanging and they're trying to understand more what's happening with the patient['s] discharge. You could be a hospitalist, and you've been off shift for like seven days, and then you come to the hospital and now the patient is on their tenth day, but you inherit that discharge. Going through, reading every progress note for every single day, reading every consult for every subspecialty that looked at this patient usually would take two to three days to actually get the patient out of the building safely," he said.

Rather than manually compiling information for a discharge summary, clinicians can use ClinicalKey AI to aggregate relevant information from across the patient’s record, trace it back to its source and review the AI-generated summary before signing off on the discharge, according to Hallak.

Sources indicate that "It is a game changer, in my opinion. One of our hospitals stated it used to take me three days to discharge a patient; now it takes me less than three hours," he said.

Sources indicate that going forward, the system expects to measure operational outcomes such as length of stay, safe discharge and multidisciplinary-rounds use, according to Hallak. The medical center also intends to evaluate clinicians' use of the tool and how it changes care decisions.

The medical center has also deployed other AI tools such as Oracle Health's clinical AI agent for ambient documentation.

Industry observers note that "These things are crucial. We're hoping to bring in a clinical AI agent for nurses as well to help the whole care team be able to eliminate the noise, the friction that typically EHRs or IT would bring to the conversation," Hallak stated.

Industry observers note that the medical center is taking a risk-based approach to AI governance, using source verification and peer review for AI-generated summaries while applying greater scrutiny to tools that are predictive or suggestive, Hallak noted. That oversight involves clinical experts as well as compliance, legal and cybersecurity teams along with traditional vendor security and product-vetting requirements.

AI governance should become stricter as the technology moves from summarizing information to recommending or taking actions, he said.

Elsevier designed ClinicalKey AI with security and trust in mind, including HIPAA compliance, citations that show where information comes from and safeguards that keep the tool from prescribing what clinicians should do. Instead, it surfaces relevant information to help clinicians make their own decisions, Lott stated.

Sources indicate that "Health systems tell us two things stand in the way of adopting AI: tools that don’t work with their existing EHR partners, and concerns about security, compliance and responsible use," Omry Bigger, president of Clinical Solutions at Elsevier, said. "ClinicalKey AI was designed to address both. As an EHR-supported and HIPAA-compliant ready solution, ClinicalKey AI integrates seamlessly across health systems to provide clinicians with trusted evidence and patient context that gives them tailored clinical insights for each patient at the point of care.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kid Harpoon’s former Los Angeles rental is ready for its next act.
  • The Grammy-winning producer, whose real name is Tom Hull, previously rented the 1957 Laurel Canyon home that’s now on the market for $2.5 million, according to listing agent Trey Alligood of Douglas Elliman.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kid Harpoon’s former Los Angeles rental is ready for its next act.

The Grammy-winning producer, whose real name is Tom Hull, previously rented the 1957 Laurel Canyon home that’s now on the market for $2.5 million, according to listing agent Trey Alligood of Douglas Elliman.

The three-bedroom property has a view of the Hollywood sign and a backyard deck that spans more than half the size of the house itself.

Harpoon rented the property as a workspace, transferring several parts of the residence into producing spaces, where he helped bring some of the biggest songs to life.

In a recent development, music fans might also recognize the street name. The house sits at 2143 Ridgemont Drive, and the credits for Miley Cyrus’ “Endless Summer Vacation” name a Los Angeles recording location called Ridgemont High.

Ridgemont Studio also appears in the credits for Harry Styles’ “Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.” Neither set of credits gives a street address, but Hull’s role in both artists’ careers is well documented.

His work on Styles’ “Harry’s House” earned him a Grammy for Album of the Year. A year later, Hull and fellow producer Tyler Johnson shared in another win when Cyrus’ “Flowers” took home Record of the Year. Hull’s contributions extended well beyond the production booth. On “Flowers,” he also played bass and drums.

Sources indicate that by Laurel Canyon standards, the producer was part of a relatively recent wave of musical talent. The house was already standing when artists including Joni Mitchell and Cass Elliot helped turn the neighborhood into a gathering place for musicians in the 1960s.

Decades later, the Grammy Museum devoted an exhibition to the people who lived and worked there, with artifacts as personal as Elliot’s hand-painted chair.

“Laurel Canyon has always pulled in creative people, and buyers feel that,” Alligood tells Realtor.com®. “When a house has real history behind it, you’re not just buying square footage, you’re buying into a story, and that’s something new construction can’t replicate.

“Homes like that stay in the conversation long after other listings have come and gone.”.

At the Ridgemont Drive property, the most generous entertaining space is out back. A 1,250-square-foot deck has its own kitchen, complete with a barbecue and refrigerator, so whoever is cooking can stay outside with guests.

A pergola shelters the fire pit, while a separate terrace gives people room to peel away from the main gathering. The 9,270-square-foot lot also accommodates a stretch of lawn and a storage shed.

Inside, the home’s midcentury design is easiest to appreciate from the living room. A sculptural fireplace anchors the space, and a bank of floor-to-ceiling Fleetwood sliders opens to the deck.

With the doors drawn back, anyone sitting by the fireplace has a clear line to the backyard.

The dining area and kitchen share that same open room.

The kitchen island gives guests a place to pull up while dinner is underway. A Thermador range handles the cooking, and there’s a wine refrigerator indoors as well as the fridge out by the grill.

Elsewhere in the 2,245-square-foot house, a dedicated office leaves all three bedrooms available for sleeping, a practical perk in a home where the main living spaces flow together.

It has been revealed that the primary suite has a backyard entrance of its own. Its sliding doors offer a direct route outside in the morning, while the adjoining bathroom gives owners a choice between a soak in the tub and a steam shower.

All of the rooms occupy a single level, and the attached two-car garage opens directly into the house.

Both bathrooms have been renovated, along with updates that range from latest hardwood flooring and lighting to fresh paint inside and out. Even the exterior wood got some attention. It was sanded and stained again. A new drip irrigation system serves the drought-tolerant landscaping.

Alligood, who holds the listing through the Alligood Group at Douglas Elliman, states buyers were already paying attention during the property’s opening week.

"As for the market, L.A. buyers are selective right now, [but] when a home is priced right and presented well, it moves fast,” he claims. “We’ve received extensive traction on this home having only been on the market a week.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, millions of renters, apartment residents, and condo owners can’t put solar on a roof they don’t control.
  • Rooftop solar assumes you own a roof, can afford a large upfront cost, and can wait through permits and installation.
  • Industry observers note that UL 3700, the Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In Photovoltaic Equipment and Systems, was published in December 2025, and UL Solutions began certifying products to it in January 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, millions of renters, apartment residents, and condo owners can’t put solar on a roof they don’t control. Plug-in solar, also called balcony solar or plug-in PV, offers a workaround: one or more panels connected through a microinverter to an ordinary wall outlet, with no roof work and, in a growing number of states, no utility interconnection application — though, this is only applicable in select states (users should refer to their state laws before installation). A fresh safety standard, UL 3700, is helping this market mature, and it comes with a lesson every buyer should learn: a compliant component is not the same thing as a certified system.

Rooftop solar assumes you own a roof, can afford a large upfront cost, and can wait through permits and installation. Plug-in solar flips that. States are responding. As of mid-October, ten states had enacted plug-in solar laws: Utah, Maine, Virginia, Colorado, Maryland, Upcoming Hampshire, Connecticut, Vermont, New Jersey, and California. Effective dates vary, with several laws not taking effect until 2027, and New York’s SUNNY Act is awaiting the governor’s signature. Several of these laws require kits to meet a recognized safety standard, and some name UL 3700.

Industry observers note that UL 3700, the Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In Photovoltaic Equipment and Systems, was published in December 2025, and UL Solutions began certifying products to it in January 2026. It exists because rooftop solar standards weren’t written for equipment that homeowners plug in themselves. The safety problems are specific:.

Recent findings suggest that hoymiles claims the HiFlow Pro was built around these challenges and shuts down in 135 milliseconds if it’s unplugged or the grid fails. For comparison, Maine’s law requires shutoff within 0.2 seconds.

According to recent reports, here is the part that matters most for buyers. UL 3700 evaluates a complete system: the microinverter, how it connects, relevant accessories, and the overall configuration, not the microinverter alone. That means compliance for one part doesn’t automatically establish that the whole kit has been certified.

The HiFlow Pro demonstrates how this works in practice. Hoymiles describes the microinverter itself as UL 3700-compliant, and it has been widely reported as the first plug-in microinverter in the US to reach that point after its July 15, 2026 launch. The complete HiFlow Pro system has not yet finished certification. Hoymiles states it is pursuing it and expects the process to wrap up in December 2026.

Industry observers note that the HiFlow Pro is a plug-in microinverter, so the panels are bought separately or as part of a kit. Per Hoymiles, up to four units can run on separate outlets for up to 1,200 watts, depending on state and local rules, and models range from 360 W to 500 W to fit different legal limits. The manufacturer lists a peak efficiency of 95.5%, a NEMA Type 6 enclosure, an operating range of -40°F to 149°F, a 12-year standard warranty, and monitoring through the S-Miles Home app. It also cites 250,000 hours of reliability testing, and says TIME named the product one of its Best Inventions of 2026.

Recent findings suggest that follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Plug the unit directly into a wall outlet, not a power strip or extension cord, and use a GFCI outlet if you’re running a larger system on one circuit.

Hoymiles estimates up to 721 kWh a year from a single 360 W unit, modeled at 5.6 peak sun hours a day and about 2,403 kWh from a four-unit system. At 38 cents per kWh, a rate found only in the highest-cost regions, the manufacturer estimates savings of up to about $247 per unit per year and a payback of roughly two years. By our math, that figure assumes about 90% of the power gets used inside the home. Actual savings depend on how much electricity you use during daylight hours, and surplus power may flow to the grid without credit unless your utility offers net metering.

Industry observers note that for context, EnergySage puts typical savings from a plug-in kit at $13 to $20 a month at the national average rate of about 18 cents per kWh, and $40 to $50 a month in high-rate states like California, New York, and Hawaii. Two limits are worth knowing: the system reduces your bill but doesn’t replace the grid, and it won’t provide backup power in an outage. The federal homeowner solar tax credit also ended on December 31, 2025, so payback estimates shouldn’t assume one.

Rules vary by state, and sometimes by utility. Hawaii, with some of the country’s highest electricity prices, isn’t among the ten states with a plug-in solar law, so renters and condo owners here should check with Hawaiian Electric and their association before buying. Even in states with laws, utilities may ask for notice, and landlord and HOA protections differ.

Prices and product configurations vary by retailer, so check the current listing.

Tesla's Safety Lawsuits Never Reach Courts Because Of The Fine Print At Purchase

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (440 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While Tesla faces legal challenges from a who's who of governmental oversight bodies, Tesla has been able to repeatedly dodge private citizens complaints through a seemingly ironclad arbitration clause found in all latest Tesla sales contracts.
  • In fact, civil lawsuits regarding deadly and damaging crashes seem to end in quiet settlement after quiet settlement.
  • Recent findings suggest that the pivotal line item can be found in customer contracts regarding forced arbitration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Tesla faces legal challenges from a who's who of governmental oversight bodies, Tesla has been able to repeatedly dodge private citizens complaints through a seemingly ironclad arbitration clause found in all latest Tesla sales contracts.

In fact, civil lawsuits regarding deadly and damaging crashes seem to end in quiet settlement after quiet settlement. When they don't, the payout is massive, like the $243 million judgement after a 2019 Autopilot crash in Florida. So what is Tesla hiding behind closed doors?

Recent findings suggest that the pivotal line item can be found in customer contracts regarding forced arbitration. As the San Francisco Chronicle points out in its investigation, Tesla quietly settled 920 consumer cases in the last 10 years; "twice as many as the nine other top 10 U.S. automakers combined." So far, in the public court records and case logs the Chronicle collected, it found Tesla managed to skirt 12 attempted class action lawsuits because of its ironclad arbitration clause.

The specific arbitration agreement under each of those sections says that if an issue isn't resolved within 60 days of occurrence, the owner agrees to have any issue resolved via arbitration. Owners are unable to bring about any class-action lawsuits against the company.

Recent findings suggest that two attorneys found that out when they were hired to take on Tesla. The initial class-action lawsuit they brought against Tesla had 12 individuals behind it which ,due to the agreement, forced it to be broken down into 12 separate arbitrations. And as is the way in arbitration, Tesla wasn't required to supply discovery evidence, especially if it considered any data "proprietary information," so the problem disappeared without any admittance of wrongdoing.

The approach works so well for Tesla that other automakers are beginning to take notice and add similar agreements to their own vehicles or taking cases into arbitration as well. Rivian, also an electric vehicle maker, has already done so.

Industry observers note that owners can at least opt out within 30 days of signing the agreement by sending a letter to a Tesla P.O. Box in Fremont, California. How many of them knew that was a possibility is likely low, as even the Chronicle found most Tesla owners had no idea it was there. To truly see the entire picture you should read the entire investigation by the Chronicle, and watch its accompanying video.

In a recent development, it's a stark reminder of how important it is to read the terms of service to everything you purchase and use before signing. Otherwise, you end up in a losing battle against Tesla, or Stan's unfortunate situation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Americans want a healthcare experience that's simpler and easier to understand, and artificial intelligence may be the key to getting there, a fresh survey shows.

The poll, conducted by the Harris Poll and commissioned by Elevance Health, found that 82% of American patients view at least some part of healthcare information as a "foreign language," and close to half (45%) stated they made a healthcare decision they later regretted due to a lack of understanding.

In a recent development, the survey was conducted among 2,0001 adults in mid-July, and 74% noted they have encountered a key barrier, such as understanding their health insurance or a medical bill. And only a quarter (27%) said they completely understand their own health coverage.

That stated, most (79%) of those surveyed said they believe AI can help to improve the healthcare experience overall.

Ratnakar Lavu, chief digital information officer at Elevance Health, told Fierce in an email that because the tech has the ability to promptly surface and parse key data about a member or health need, it can serve as a central piece of the puzzle in making a more personalized experience.

It has been revealed that "AI-enabled tools give us the ability to create a unique member context," he stated. "Because of this digital technology, we can now truly 'know the person' and proactively work with them to help them manage their healthcare needs.".

For example, 82% of those surveyed said they would like to receive answers about healthcare as quickly as they can use an app to order a food delivery, and 83% would like to easily access recommendations that pull from their health coverage, individual health needs and financial situation.

Seventy-two percent remarked they would trust AI for accuracy on at least one type of information, such as an explanation of benefits, cost estimates or details on medication.

However, while many Americans believe AI can play a leading role in driving a better health experience, just 20% mentioned they currently use the tech regularly as a source of information. And while 72% said they trusted the tech to surface key health information, 33% said they would trust an AI platform to translate their insurance benefits, and 30% said they trust the tech to estimate care costs.

Just 13% mentioned they would trust AI to make diagnoses.

Lavu stated that healthcare organizations looking to roll out latest tools need to avoid simply embedding AI into programs for the sake of it, and be transparent about both the use case as well as the role of the human in the loop.

The study also found that women were less likely than men to trust AI, and younger generations were more likely to use it as a source of healthcare information than older groups.

Recent findings suggest that "We have to implement AI at the speed of trust, which means being thoughtful about where AI adds value, not just delivering technology for technology’s sake," he noted. "Trust is also earned when AI-enabled programs truly make things easier for the consumer. ".

For example, Elevance Health has deployed an AI-powered program to support utilization management reviews and help drive faster approvals where possible, though AI is not used to make claims denials. It is also leaning on AI for more proactive member engagement initiatives through its digital channels, identifying individuals that would benefit from extra support or who may face gaps in care.

"We start by listening to members and identifying where healthcare is creating the most confusion or friction," Lavu noted. "From there, we determine the right solution, which may or may not involve AI. When AI is the right tool, it should fit naturally into familiar interactions and make it easier for members to get an answer or take the next step.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Audi Sport has put out an incredible amount of renowned performance cars over the years, but without a doubt the most beloved by enthusiasts are the various RS Avants. From the original RS2 to the RS4 and RS6, the Avant wagons have far outweighed sedans when it comes to production volume and cultural impact, even if you count the recent four-door RS5s. Some generations of RS4 and RS6 never even received sedan variants, and the last RS6 sedan (the V10-powered C6) went out of production in 2010. That role was filled by the RS7 four-door coupe, and there's no more A7 anymore, either.

It has been revealed that for the upcoming RS6 version of the current C9-gen A6, which has been running around testing in camouflage for quite a long time now, Audi is bringing back the RS6 sedan in addition to the Avant. Our spies took a upcoming batch of shots of the RS6 sedan looking even closer to production while testing at the Nürburgring, looking particularly bodacious with its widebody clearly visible despite the camo wrap. To assuage the worries I know are swirling around in your brains, Audi already confirmed the new RS6 Avant will come to America, so the sedan will just be another flavor to choose from if, for some reason, you're someone who hates wagons like those people who say they have an anti-cilantro gene.

This RS6 sedan prototype doesn't have any fake body panels or other earlier-stage camouflage coverings, with the only thing obfuscating the design being the swirly wrap. The upcoming RS5 is wider than a regular A5 by over 1.5 inches, and the same looks to be true for the RS6. Like the RS5, its larger sibling also has a functional vent in the front fenders ahead of the door, and the flared arches are filled with big wheels that look to be 22s.

Recent findings suggest that it's got a similar double-diamond pattern to the wide front grille, and the side intakes in the RS6's front bumper look even bigger than the RS5's. Camo is covering the headlights, which will get RS-specific running light designs and animations. There's a cute little lip spoiler on the trunk, and the rear diffuser has two gigantic oval exhaust tips. The taillights should also have RS designs.

According to recent reports, the yellow sticker on the rear window confirms that the RS6 will be a plug-in hybrid, and while early rumors and prototypes pointed to the RS6 using the same twin-turbo V6 as the RS5, we know it will use an updated version of the Porsche-derived V8 that's in the current gas-only RS6 (and that's used in PHEV Porsches and Bentleys). With a large battery pack and an electric motor added on, the new RS6 should have at least 700 horsepower and a usable EV range of a few dozen miles. We'll find out for sure when the RS6 debuts at some point in 2027.

#145257. Seabed Mining Has a Refinery Problem Worth Billions

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1002 w)
