Seabed Mining Has a Refinery Problem Worth Billions

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Metals Company wants to recover polymetallic nodules from the seabed and sell the nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese they contain.
  • That gap belongs in the mining economics.
  • Offshore collection gets the attention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Metals Company wants to recover polymetallic nodules from the seabed and sell the nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese they contain. That business needs an industrial processing system before its revenue projections become sales. TMC’s November 2026 update exposed the timing problem. Its proposed refinery complex in Brownsville, Texas, may not be operating when offshore collection begins. An established Japanese smelter operated by Pacific Metals, or PAMCO, is the prospective initial route, but it needs modifications to accept commercial volumes of nodules.

That gap belongs in the mining economics. TMC’s 2025 prefeasibility study allocated $4.426 billion to two proposed US hydrometallurgical refineries, about 89% of the study’s $4.971 billion of initial project capital. The denominator has a particular financing structure: the offshore amount covers the first collection system after an Allseas capital credit, while later systems are to be supplied through contracts and paid for through operating costs. The newer Brownsville proposal also has a different industrial scope. The 2025 figure reveals the size of the processing business TMC’s economics must support, not a completed financing commitment for Brownsville.

Offshore collection gets the attention. Refineries decide what saleable material a collection system produces and who captures its value. A nodule delivered to port is a complex mineral feedstock, not a sale of four finished metals. One processing route smelts nodules into a nickel-copper-cobalt alloy and manganese silicate, converts the alloy into matte and refines the matte into marketable metals or chemicals. The manganese product needs customers or additional treatment. Each step consumes capital, energy, reagents, skilled labor and working capital.

TMC has a meaningful metallurgical program. Its third-quarter 2026 SEC filing describes earlier North American tests of about 70 tons of nodules and a 2,000-ton industrial demonstration at PAMCO’s Hachinohe facility. Further work at SGS in Canada tested the refining of intermediate material into battery-grade products. PAMCO has completed feasibility work on treating roughly 1.3 million wet tons per year through a modified existing facility. That is a stronger starting point than a conceptual processing flowsheet.

According to recent reports, the November 12 corporate update nevertheless put the industrial dependency in plain view. TMC’s preferred Brownsville facility will be difficult to complete before the first commercial nodules arrive, and the Japanese facility requires modifications and aligned schedules. Korea Zinc, Glencore, Hatch, Mariana Minerals and other partners provide useful expertise and commercial relationships. Those relationships still leave the construction, commissioning, financing and refining arrangements to complete.

The value gap matters as much as the capital bill. In our 2025 seabed mining techno-economic assessment, metallurgist Lyle Trytten and I calculated a $553-per-ton contained-component reference value for representative Clarion-Clipperton Zone nodules at fixed historical metal prices. Using estimated purchase terms informed by analogous mineral markets, the same assessment gave a modeled raw-feed value of $188–256 per ton, or about 34–46% of that contained reference value.

It has been revealed that the gap pays for real industrial work. Processors bear metal recovery losses, treatment costs, plant capital, financing, product quality and operating risk, and they need a return. The values are estimates on a common reference basis, not bids from refineries or the profit a processor would pocket. Commercial nodule tonnage is often reported wet; TMC’s study assumes 28% moisture. Feed-price comparisons with wet-ton mine costs require the same mass basis.

The mining organization has three main choices. It can sell the raw nodules at a price a processor can afford. It can keep title to the material and pay a plant to process it, provided the contract sets capacity, treatment charges, recoveries and risk allocation. Or it can finance and operate refining facilities and pursue a larger portion of the finished-metal revenue. None transfers the work, capital and risk out of the industrial system.

Sources indicate that TMC’s own operating estimates reinforce that point. The 2025 study projected $13.622 billion of lifetime processing costs and $3.254 billion of refining costs, together about $103 per wet ton, or 42% of its modeled operating expenditure. Those costs sit alongside the proposed refinery capital. The production system may be offshore, but the economic center of gravity reaches well into the onshore industrial chain.

Sources indicate that impossible Metals has a different, less developed processing position. Its published strategy begins with outsourcing to modified plants in allied countries and envisions dedicated facilities later. Its economic model used approximately $791 per ton of contained-metal value under its selected prices and grades, deducted a $230 processing charge, and arrived at roughly $560 per ton delivered to port. Those numbers use different input assumptions from our assessment and cannot be treated as a direct comparison with the $188–256 estimate. The commercial question is whether a processor would accept the feedstock and the risks on the terms in Impossible Metals’ model.

Existing nickel-processing projects offer warning enough. Ravensthorpe, Goro and Ambatovy had familiar metallurgical technologies yet encountered expensive commissioning and operational difficulties. An unusual feedstock, high-volume throughput, uncertain manganese outlets and synchronized offshore and onshore ramp-up add challenges for nodule ventures. Demonstrating that the chemistry works settles only one part of the investment case.

TMC has considerably more testing and more developed partners than Impossible Metals. That distinction matters. Neither has demonstrated a fully operating processing chain that delivers the required metals at its intended scale, recovery, capital cost and commercial terms. Government financing could change who carries part of the risk, but not what must be built or operated.

It has been revealed that A seabed mining tech giant cannot book finished-metal economics while making the refinery somebody else’s problem. Investors, taxpayers and prospective processing partners need to know who provides the billions in capital, who carries the ramp-up risk and how much of the metal value the collector retains after every participant has been paid.

It has been revealed that my full TFIE Strategy Briefing article follows the processing alternatives, TMC’s Japanese and US looks, Impossible Metals’ outsourcing assumptions, and the resulting revenue and investment gaps. It is the third article in a five-part seabed mining assessment.

Navigating the world of Google Ads can be challenging, especially in an industry as competitive as real estate. One term you've probably heard in relation to Google Ads is "Quality Score." This score is crucial to how your ads perform and how much they cost. But what does it mean for realtors, and what constitutes a great Google Quality Real Estate Score? Let's dive in.

It has been revealed that google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

However, remember that Quality Score is just one piece of the puzzle. You should also consider other factors like your bidding strategy and overall account performance to create a successful Google Ads campaign.

With continuous effort and strategic planning, you can optimize your Quality Score and ultimately generate more leads for your real estate business.

CMS to withdraw moratorium on new ACA broker registrations" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

It has been revealed that UPDATED: Nov 20 at 1:30 p.m. ET.

The Trump administration has agreed to withdraw its moratorium on latest broker enrollments, court documents show.

Sources indicate that according to a filing submitted Thursday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Service will published a withdrawal on the Federal Register. The move follows a court ruling earlier this month in favor of two leading organizations representing brokers, which granted a preliminary injunction on the moratorium.

Recent findings suggest that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America both sued over the regulation. NABIP argued that the moratorium would have a significant impact on licensed professionals operating in accordance with the law.

Per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

UPDATED: Nov. 5 at 4:30 p.m. ET.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on upcoming broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act.".

The court also mentioned that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

NABIP noted that the ruling means that it will restart training for newly introduced brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

"Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," said NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters.".

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," mentioned Walker.

Recent findings suggest that NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

Sources indicate that PUBLISHED: Oct. 15 at 5:15 p.m. ET.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on latest brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency said it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency mentioned newly introduced brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP indicates that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment.".

Recent findings suggest that the organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP said.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization stated.

NABIP President Mychal Walker stated that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker noted in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them.".

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

In a recent development, CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA plans without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are currently listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while many in the US are celebrating Thanksgiving, I am seeing some of the most advanced technology and most impressive EVs in the world.
  • After renewing my Chinese driving permit, I was able to drive the sporty P7 again and use NGP with VLA 2.0 to and from XPENG’s increasingly automated and clean factory.
  • I also had the opportunity to ride in the YoYo Robotaxi with my friend Dan Caesar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while many in the US are celebrating Thanksgiving, I am seeing some of the most advanced technology and most impressive EVs in the world. XPENG offered to bring me to see AI day and Auto Guangzhou. I am thankful for the opportunity. Expect to hear more in depth in the days to come.

After renewing my Chinese driving permit, I was able to drive the sporty P7 again and use NGP with VLA 2.0 to and from XPENG’s increasingly automated and clean factory. That is simply a great car to drive. Acceleration is smooth and powerful. Despite the motor torque, the chassis can more than handle it. It feels both connected and comfortable in a balance that can be hard to find in many cars. And it looks great, especially in the dark green of the test car. I wish I had time to take it to some twisty backroads. However, the intelligent driving system makes dense urban traffic far more tolerable. At the times when you don’t want to drive, NGP drives the car flawlessly. Over the past year I have seen the system evolve, and it now offers even greater perception, smoothness, and efficiency. It is something you must experience to fully appreciate.

I also had the opportunity to ride in the YoYo Robotaxi with my friend Dan Caesar. Compared to some other robotaxi systems, it is a definite step up in comfort. More like limo service than a traditional taxi. The driving is extremely smooth, as is the ride, even in the congested and unpredictable roads in China. It drives much better than a typical human or some of the competitors I sampled. With the seat reclined, massage on and excellent entertainment system playing music or movies, I didn’t want to leave. I could have used another lap. I’ll have more details soon.

The following day, I attended XPENG AI Day. Over the course of the multi-hour event and Q&A, the amount of technological progress I was exposed to was expansive. Not only did I get to hear in depth about all the technological developments at XPENG, but I also was able to ask the IRON humanoid robot a question. With roughly half of the organization dedicated to R&D, the speed of progress is impressive.

It has been revealed that during the presentation, I heard about major developments in intelligent driving, including innovations that increase efficiency and range. I also heard about milestones being accomplished in flying cars, which took off in a demonstration the next day. However, the humanoid robot walking in to demonstrate the progress ahead of mass production clearly attracted the most attention.

Industry observers note that I would like to think that I have a better understanding of these topics than many people, given the experience I have had so far. But the new helping of ideas and concepts was too much for me to process. My brain feels completely stuffed. Like that extra helping of Thanksgiving dinner, it will take a little bit for me to digest everything I have seen. Keep an eye out for more in-depth reports.

Industry observers note that however, information was not the only thing I was gorging myself on. The food is exceptionally good in Guangzhou. While I have had great food at restaurants here, my favorite food is at the XPENG headquarters cafeteria at Mom’s Kitchen. This program lets the parents of employees set up shop to sell food at the cafeteria. As many employees come from different parts of the country, the program gives  them a taste of home. I am not sure what the dishes that I was eating were called, but there is something simply better about a home cooked meal. It may not look fancy, but the flavors were amazing. In addition, the hotel had turkey available for dinner, so I didn’t miss out on food.

I also was able to explore some Fall foliage. However, the leaves do not change color here in Guangzhou. Flowers are in bloom year-round, giving it the nickname “Flower City.” As I had done the standard headquarters tour before, I was able to split off with Tanya of XPENG to explore the grounds. Next to the headquarters building is a park with running trails, a pond and a river running through it, including a small waterfall. Throughout the year, there are events in the park, including concerts.

What is particularly impressive in the park is that much of this was bare dirt from the construction of XPENG’s headquarters when I visited in last November. Over the past year, grass, plants and trees were planted. The river was cleaned up to be clean and clear, with people fishing in its waters. Something that I would not imagine doing in most urban rivers. The planting is still in progress, but the environmental restoration is already impressive. And it is a reminder of how key it is to balance industry with nature.

In a recent development, on days that are not too hot, employees will often take their lunches outside or even take out mats to take a nap on the lawn. As the trees grow in further, the shade will increase and improve the comfort further. The park is also open to the public, and you can often see children playing. I heard the most difficult part is that people wish they had more time to enjoy the park. But XPENG has been remarkably busy.

It has been revealed that tomorrow, is Black Friday. A day dedicated to buying stuff. However, I will be at Auto Guangzhou looking at a wide range of exciting vehicles that I can’t buy in the United States. Better cars that are better because they are EVs. Cutting edge technology, premium amenities, and impressive build quality at affordable prices. Vehicles that give you newly introduced perspective on what’s possible.

Recent findings suggest that I was able to see clear progress in the industry from the show last November to the Beijing show in April. Although XPENG is launching their models globally, many other brands launch in their home market first. Seeing the speed, progress and competition is invigorating having come from a market that often feels like it is stalling, but it can also be a bit overwhelming. I feel lucky to have the opportunity to see it firsthand and hope I can give people a glimpse of what’s happening.

In a recent development, overall, I feel thankful for the opportunities to see and experience the some of the most advanced clean technology in the world over the past year with CleanTechnica. I am especially thankful to XPENG for being so open about their technology and the underlying thinking. It has been enlightening to see how the progress is being made in China and how that progress is being brought to Europe. I thank the PR teams for taking such good care of me and answering my questions. I am also thankful to Jackery for showing me innovations in energy storage and solar that create solutions for customer needs in both the US and Europe. And I am also thankful for BMW showing me something to be hopeful about regarding EVs and manufacturing in the US.

Recent findings suggest that I am also thankful for all the great people I have met. From technology leaders to media legends, I have consistently been impressed. I now often feel like I am visiting friends. Business travel can feel lonely, but I have rarely felt that this year.

Recent findings suggest that I am thankful for our readers, who make this possible. I often feel like I am learning from their comments as much as they are learning from what I write.

And I am thankful for my wife for putting up with all my nerdy conversations and trips away from home. And I am thankful for my cats, who are always happy to see me. I’ll be home soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, according to its ad, today's Nice Price or No Dice Vega was once a door prize on the TV game show, "The Price Is Right." Today, it appears nicely restored and has a surprise SBC under its hood. Let's see if any of you are game to pay its asking price.

It has been revealed that A common way to describe avoidance of an object or idea is the phrase "I wouldn't touch it with a 10-foot pole." The origin of this idiom remains unknown, but a similar, earlier phrase, "not to be handled with a pair of tongs," carries the same meaning. In 18th-century Great Britain, 10-foot was frequently substituted with "barge," as barge poles were typically long and thus offered reasonably remote poking opportunities.

I bring this all up because, based on the comments, the 2017 Alfa Romeo Giulia we looked at on Wednesday was a car that some of you wouldn't touch with a 10-foot pole. That was because the car—and Alfa Romeo in general—carries a reputation for frustratingly frequent breakdowns and bank-account-bruising repairs. That being said, our Giulia's great looks, seemingly good condition, and $7,999 asking price proved a winning combination in the end. That's shown by the 70% 'Nice Price' win it received in the vote.

Industry observers note that while not as good-looking as yesterday's Alfa, the 1973 Chevy Vega notchback that stands before us today is an arguably handsome, well-balanced design. The car's mini-Camaro nose and pleasing profile were the best things about it when it debuted in 1970. Pretty much everything else about the car, however, was snake-bit from the start.

Chevrolet introduced the Vega in late summer 1970 as the brand's new compact car, nominally replacing the Corvair, which had ended its production run a year earlier. Like the Corvair, the Vega was a clean-sheet design, sharing little carryover parts from other GM cars. Also like the Corvair, the Vega proved problematic for the brand.

According to recent reports, the complications that plagued the early model years weren't limited to engineering or production mistakes; even the car's innovative transportation method—shipping it vertically on specially designed train cars—caused unforeseen fluid leaks before the Vegas even reached a dealer. Premature corrosion was another Vega bugaboo, especially in rustbelt states. The biggest problem, though, was with the Vega's SOHC 2.3-liter four-cylinder engine. Built with an alloy block and cast iron head, the engine had no cylinder liners or special wear-resistant coating to keep the bores intact. Chevrolet had to problem recalls on almost every Vega produced to address safety and drivability issues after only two years of production.

Fortunately, someone has addressed at least the engine problems with this Vega by sending its original motor to the recycler and replacing it with a 350 cubic inch small-block Chevy V8. Could there be a more reliable engine than the tried-and-true SBC?

In a recent development, that engine looks right at home in the Vega's engine bay and sits unencumbered by unnecessary ancillaries like a power steering pump or an air conditioning compressor. It does have a heater hookup and a larger-than-stock radiator to cool the plus-size engine. Other engine bay items of note include an MDS distributor and coil and a custom brazed-together air intake that flops the filter over one rocker cover.

It has been revealed that based on the underneath pictures, the V8 feeds what looks to be the Vega's Opel-sourced four-speed manual gearbox and punky factory rear end, so don't expect dramatics at the drag strip out of this car. According to the ad, the car has around 90,000 miles on the clock, but only a couple thousand of those were added after the engine swap. The seller claims it " Drives great and turns heads.".

In a recent development, A fresh engine isn't the only update this Vega has seen. At the same time as the heart transplant, this car also got new candy-apple red paint and fresh vinyl seat upholstery. The remaining original parts of the interior—door cards, dash, and carpets—all look to be in suitably good shape. Two cracks, oddly at exactly 12 and 6, mar the factory two-spoke steering wheel, but shouldn't affect its use or safety. The only other potential misstep is a modern stereo head unit that spoils the overall old-school aesthetic.

On the exterior, all the chrome shines nicely, and the paint appears to be a professionally applied respray. A set of Minilite-esque alloys underpins, and they appear to have reasonably newly introduced rubber. As is typical of Facebook Marketplace ads, the ad doesn't mention the car's title status, but given how old of a car it is, we might be able to overlook that.

It has been revealed that as noted, the ad claims this Vega had a run-in with Bob Barker on the daytime TV game show "The Price Is Right." Amazingly, that show gave away a ton of Vegas, though a quick search of the videos I could find from the era didn't turn up any featuring this particular car. We'll just have to imagine that experience, along with the opportunity to win a Tappan range or an all-inclusive seven-day adventure to Bali.

Once we're done with all that, we'll have to come back to reality and decide whether this V8 Vega is worth its $17,000 asking price. Yes, no one would have guessed that on The Price Is Right, but that's what makes this an even more exciting opportunity.

What do you think? Is this refreshed, re-engined Vega worth $17,000 as-is? Or for that price, would you refuse to "come on down!".

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Recent findings suggest that much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA proposal Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth remarked in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations.".

The star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage plans and listed on the Medicare strategy finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

It has been revealed that "The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A blueprint’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive.".

It has been revealed that UPDATED: Nov. 9 at 2:30 p.m. ET.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The tech giant sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the tech giant noted that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination.".

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the company noted.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company remarked.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance noted.

Sources indicate that "An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the tech giant continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing intends.".

UPDATED: Oct. 27 at 2:45 p.m. ET.

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

In a recent development, the court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

Industry observers note that the company stated that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement.".

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the manufacturer's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like.".

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in prepares with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

It has been revealed that in a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the tech giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene claims that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the organization, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in looks with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company noted in the lawsuit.

CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 plan year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene remarked.

"Beyond the financial impact to the firm and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company noted in the complaint.

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Recent findings suggest that PUBLISHED: Oct. 12 at 3 p.m. ET.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer notes that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to blueprint payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment mentioned in the lawsuit.

According to recent reports, the organization adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the company noted. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute.".

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

Industry observers note that in addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in looks with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the firm tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, noted that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment stated in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings.".

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the organization remarked.

  • For some of his buyers, it’s enough acreage to put real distance between them and the neighbors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mauricio Umansky has a read on what makes a multimillion-dollar home irresistible.

For some of his buyers, it’s enough acreage to put real distance between them and the neighbors. For others, it’s the luxury of stepping into a sauna or taking a cold plunge without leaving home.

“Privacy is becoming a bigger priority for luxury buyers,” The Agency founder revealed while speaking to Mansion Global.

He mentioned buyers are drawn to properties where they can retreat from view, feel secure, and build a wellness routine around amenities such as a private gym or spa.

Umansky is putting his read on the market to work in Miami’s Edgewater neighborhood, where he is leading sales for HQ Residences Miami.

The project brings together singer Marc Anthony, hospitality entrepreneur Sam Nazarian, and SBE. Its pitch borrows from the hotel world, pairing private residences with wellness amenities, places for neighbors to gather, and an emphasis on service.

Industry observers note that even at the top of the market, buyers are watching what they pay. Umansky remarked there’s room to negotiate in some areas, while a well-priced home in a coveted location can still draw strong interest.

He recommended finding an agent who knows the neighborhood and being ready to act when a property comes along that you can see yourself living in for years.

Umansky’s own homes span Los Angeles, La Quinta, CA, and Aspen, CO.

Los Angeles gives him access to city life, while La Quinta offers the appeal of a slower pace, sunny days, and a round of golf. In Aspen, the draw extends from ski season to summers in the mountains and the sense of community he finds there.

If he were to add another address, Umansky noted he could picture himself in Europe.

He singled out the South of France, Italy, and Spain, with particular affection for Madrid. Miami also appeals to him as a place to own a home, especially after spending more time in the city through his work on HQ Residences.

The broker also reflected on what TV has done for his business. Appearances on “Buying Beverly Hills,” “Dancing With the Stars,” and “Special Forces” have introduced him to people he might never have met through real estate alone, he said, and brought more attention to The Agency.

Recent findings suggest that the trade-off is that some people form an impression of him from what they see on camera. He mentioned he wants his reputation to rest on his work as an agent and the trust he earns from clients.

As for the prospect of running for mayor, Umansky spoke about what he would focus on if he pursued the job.

According to recent reports, “Los Angeles is my home, and I care deeply about its future,” he told Mansion Global. He said he’d look at how the city handles housing approvals and development, with the goal of making it easier to build and attracting more investment and jobs.

Sources indicate that the candid glimpse into what wealthy buyers want comes one week after his stepdaughter, Farrah Aldjufrie—who is also Kyle Richards' daughter—gave birth to a baby boy. The arrival came three months after Aldjufrie revealed the baby's father is Zach Goldsmith, her "Buying Beverly Hills" co-star and fellow The Agency agent.

The 37-year-old property mogul, who is the daughter of Richards and her ex-husband, Guraish Aldjufrie, shared the news in July that she was expecting her first child.

Then, one month later, she hard-rolled out her relationship with Goldsmith while sharing a video of the two of them celebrating their gender reveal.

A source told Page Six that the TV alum has welcomed her son, though Aldjufrie has yet to confirm the news herself.

The pregnancy marked a joyful personal milestone for the real estate mogul, whose professional achievements have often played out in front of TV audiences.

Recent findings suggest that aldjufrie had previously revealed how Umansky helped to cultivate her love of real estate. In a 2016 interview with The Daily Dish, she said that as a child, she used to drive around L.A. with her stepfather to tour listings, fascinated by everything that went into selling them.

According to recent reports, “I always have been interested in real estate since I was a little kid. I’d drive around to open houses with my mom and Mauricio when I was 6, 7, 8 years old. I’d love to see all the houses,” she mentioned.

According to recent reports, “I know L.A. geographically really, really well, having grown up here. I was an only child for the first eight years, so I spent a lot of time with them and was very interested in everything Mauricio was doing. But I have my own love for property and being in L.A. There's some of the most amazing properties and lifestyles in the world.”.

According to her profile on The Agency's website, Aldjufrie became an agent in 2013—and has since helped the company to achieve "over $5 billion in real estate sales.".

Interestingly, while she continues her professional and personal relationship with The Agency's founder, Umansky, her mother made clear just a few months ago that she believes she is entitled to a significant chunk of her estranged husband's empire—telling her Bravo co-stars that she will fight to claim her half of the business that she says she helped to build should the couple end up filing for divorce.

Umansky founded The Agency alongside Billy Rose and Blair Chang in 2011, 15 years after he wed Richards. By May 2022, the business had facilitated more than $57 billion in real estate sales, according to Forbes.

According to The Agency's website, the manufacturer operates more than 145 offices in 14 countries, while Umansky's bio notes that he has "achieved nearly $5 billion in real estate sales and holds the distinction of selling the most homes in the country priced above $20 million.

"He has represented some of the world's most noteworthy properties, including the Playboy Mansion—the first house in L.A. to sell above the $100 million mark—the Walt Disney Estate, and residences owned by Michael Jackson, Michael Jordan and Prince.".

Indeed, in the 15 years since it was founded, The Agency has built up a wealth of clients, including Lady Gaga, LeBron James, and Ben Affleck.

While it's unclear whether Richards would seek to be involved in the day-to-day running of the business that she hopes to claim a 50% share in, it's likely that she could be in line for a hefty payout if Umansky wishes to keep The Agency to himself.

However, Richards noted that she isn't quite ready to pull the plug on their marriage once and for all.

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

According to recent reports, for one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will enhancement application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for fresh entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for new entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give aims greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs aims.

According to recent reports, in addition, the agency remarked it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low.".

CMS is also aiming to update the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," mentioned CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health.".

In a recent development, the proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS noted, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy noted in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs.".

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there is an vital subtext to this Thanksgiving Day in the United States.
  • It has been revealed that former White House communication director Dan Pfeiffer argues this is not only possible, it is necessary.
  • Thanksgiving has long been celebrated as a way to assimilate immigrants into our national melting pot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there is an vital subtext to this Thanksgiving Day in the United States. A “blue tsunami” has occurred, so, come January, the Democratic party will control the House of Representatives and the Senate. While there are many important elements to this upheaval, one thread connects them all: Democrats can reimagine both how they govern and how they communicate.

It has been revealed that former White House communication director Dan Pfeiffer argues this is not only possible, it is necessary. The Democrats, he notes, must “make sure voters know that we tried like hell and that Republicans are to blame for the lack of progress.” Part of a successful communication strategy would involve embracing others across the political aisle. And what better time is there than Thanksgiving Day and the long weekend that follows?

Thanksgiving has long been celebrated as a way to assimilate immigrants into our national melting pot. Why not use the US holiday as a jumping off point to acknowledge the various celebrations that draw upon commonality of white American traditions, like turkey and stuffing — but also invite individual expressions of food and traditions from the diaspora? If we all would be more open to latest ideas and their origins, wouldn’t the next steps be to open up conversations and insights into sustainability and equity?

It has been revealed that we use labels because there’s so much information in the world that we can’t process each piece of it individually. The tendency to resort to labels is part of the psychological shortcuts we take to make sense of the world. So we group things and people together, and we attach labels to them. Labels help us to limit our time and attention instead of analyzing small details.

According to recent reports, nonetheless, when we label a person, we simplify the way we represent them in our brains. Labeling can create misunderstandings and stereotypes. On this Thanksgiving Day, let’s consider how the labels we place easily and quickly on others diminish our potential for social awareness and awakenings. Instead of succumbing to labels, let’s give thanks for the vibrant palette of people and cultures that surround us. In doing so, we enrich our lives and, by extension, the lives of those around us.

In a recent development, in fact, disparate cultures with differing politics often find commonality when they sit down to eat. Food scholar and Williams College professor Darra Goldstein says, “Quite apart from sustaining us, food has the ability to unite us.” She spoke at gastronomical lectures hosted earlier this autumn at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

Recent findings suggest that and there’s photographer Jeremy Dennis’s exhibition, “The Course of Liberty,” at a new alternative space in Salem, Massachusetts called Airtight Garage. The exhibition provides a corrective to years of simplified myth-making, and his staged photographic compositions feature Native Americans in traditional clothing and unexpected settings. It is as if they have broken through a time-space continuum.

Think back to the fabled tale of scraggly European Pilgrim outcasts arriving on the eastern Atlantic shore. As Florida columnist JC Bruce laughs, “If you were an indigenous person living on the North American continent in 1621 and a bunch of religious zealots revealed up with pasty skin and ridiculous clothing, would you think they were any odder than beings from the stars?”.

It has been revealed that “The Course of Liberty” questions what happens when two people claim the same space. As Cate McQuaid describes in the Boston Globe, the artist points to ideas of inherited history and reconciliation as Native people attempt to recover Native land.

Sources indicate that yes, we may need a lot more communication breakthroughs and backdoor discussions of sustainability and equity in the lead up to the January shift of Congress. But it’s not the first time such a moment in time has occurred in the US.

In a recent development, in 1864 President Abraham Lincoln reflected on the civil war. He saw a nation now dedicated “to the cause of freedom and humanity, and to afford to us reasonable hopes of an ultimate and happy deliverance from all our dangers and afflictions.”.

So let’s celebrate on this Thanksgiving Day 2026 the birthday of cartoonist Charles Shultz, who mentioned, “The best theology is probably no theology; just love one another.” Let’s do our best to live up to his ideal; good things will surely result if we do.

Photon, a prescription infrastructure tech giant, is now available as a plugin for ChatGPT to streamline prescribing for clinicians within a tool they already use.

It has been revealed that the option is available to eligible U.S. licensed clinicians using ChatGPT for Clinicians (free for verified clinicians) or ChatGPT for Healthcare. Just as clinicians must accept OpenAI’s BAA before sharing protected patient information, they must accept Photon’s BAA to maintain HIPAA compliance when using Photon in ChatGPT. Controlled substances are not supported. The feature is free for clinicians through Dec. 31, 2026.

The patient experience remains the same through Photon. What is latest is where the clinician can write a prescription. Clinicians with a Photon account can draft, review and send prescriptions without leaving ChatGPT. They just need to add the Photon plugin into ChatGPT, and then they can draft prescriptions. A patient will get a text to Photon’s prescription marketplace outside of ChatGPT. Patients can compare prices and request to change a pharmacy as needed.

“AI is moving from note-taking and reference into treatment workflows. Clinicians are already using ChatGPT to understand treatment options. Once they’ve decided what to prescribe, they should be able to act on that decision in the same conversation,” Otto Sipe, co-founder and CEO, wrote to Fierce Healthcare in an emailed comment. “Photon provides the infrastructure behind that step.”.

It has been revealed that in the upcoming interface, clinicians begin a prompt with the name of the patient and medication. Photon uses authorized patient information and treatment context shared with ChatGPT to help prepare a prescription for a clinician’s review. They can also add new patient details during the process. Once saved in Photon, that patient can be found by name for future prescriptions.

Recent findings suggest that from there, clinicians review the prescribing details, including the dosing, instructions and quantity. Clinicians can ask about dosing options in the chat. Patient records are saved in Photon, and draft prescriptions are checked against the patient’s recorded allergies and medications. Finally, clinicians review and authorize the prescription to be sent, remaining responsible for the treatment. Clinicians can check a prescription’s status in ChatGPT.

Happy Thanksgiving! Why are you reading Jalopnik instead of hanging out with your family? They never see you, you know. You barely even call. How bad could one holiday really— oh, woof. That bad, huh? Well, okay, you can hide out in the bathroom a little longer. Don't worry, I'll keep you company with a nice long blog about the automakers our readers are most thankful for.

Earlier this week, I asked you all for the automakers you've been most thankful for over the past year. Today we're looking through your answers, from Mazda to Audi to Smart. About a million of you suggested Mazda, actually, but you can't all end up in the blog. I'm sorry. We're going for a broad range of brands here, so you've got some unique things to think about while you hide away from the political arguments happening over the dinner table. Good luck with that.

Sources indicate that mazda, for the last decade and a bit they're the only brand that tried to inject fun into everything they made. Sure they didnt have a dedicated sports car outside the Miata, and sure they didnt pile up numbers and records for performance but everything from the 3 to the CX9 was on the spirited side of the coin for the segment.

Not to mention they offered, general, affordability without sacrificing options or comforts.

Lexus. My daughter got a job at a Lexus dealership as the Delivery Specialist nine and years ago. Two years later I co-signed for her to lease an NX 300 through an employee lease bonus program. She never missed a payment and three years later leased an NX 350 by herself, having built herself a solid very good credit score. And since then, she's leased a third one. She also was promoted to Customer Relations manager in '22, which she still is to this day. I started working at the same dealership six years ago. It's an excellent dealership network and an excellent product. It's been very good for my career as well. But the best part is watching my daughter go from Job to Career under the same roof, we're both managers in departments that work side by side. So I have a great deal of gratitude for the brand. Plus I leased an NX 350h for my wife, it kept her very safe during a head-on collision (low/mid speed, but still). Very grateful for the rigidity.

My VW Bug got me into working on cars, and pushing them to their limits (it's more fun to drive a slow car fast than a fast car slow). But these days it's all Audi. The one who started it all with QUATTRO! Owned many and great cars to fling around in the snow.

In a recent development, for me Alfa Romeo. I mean who else has spent so many decades building beautiful, often affordable cars. There's just something when you look at them that other cars don't have.

According to recent reports, smart. It was the first automaker I was truly invested in as a teenage car enthusiast. I fell in love with them at 15, and by the time I was 16, I could practically recite the car's brochure to you. It was the car that taught me that, to be a car enthusiast, you weren't required to love the latest Ferrari or Lamborghini. What you love is what you love. I probably wouldn't be the car person I am today if it weren't for that brand.

Submitted by: Mercedes Streeter.

It has been revealed that this year it's Toyota. This has actually been one of the few periods in my life where I haven't owned a Honda. My 5th gen 4R has been pretty rock solid. I'm going to have to do the belt, plugs, and a few other things soon but that's due to 100k miles. I'm thankful for the forward facing V6 making my life easy to replace those items.

Small companies like Rivian and maybe Subaru who still think it's crucial to build cars people want to buy and work for your business. Massive companies like GM, Ford and Tesla just want to impress investors with quarterly profits with little regard as to what people need or want.

Submitted by: Jimboy II, The Sequel.

What I am thankful for is that they have shifted the conversation.

For at least a decade, the conversation has been. "This vehicle can do more than any other vehicle. Sure costs more, but don't you want the ability to tow the Titanic through the Darien Gap while surrounded by unicorn leather and listening to a 98 speaker 10,000 watt system?".

Then Slate notes "Hey it's cheap. Maybe that's not enough for you, but it's enough for many and it's a lot more affordable.".

Recent findings suggest that ford has already responded with the Fathom. I expect other manufacturers will also respond with less expensive offerings that are lower in capabilities and luxuries, but still might be a good fit for people.

So, although I am unsure if Slate will survive and thrive, I am thankful that the conversation of what makes a good vehicle has shifted from crap most people don't need to a focus on what they actually need.

Industry observers note that fiat. For providing long time ago my favorite all time car, the Fiat X1/9 but also putting a smile on my face since 2012 with the Abarth 500!

Submitted by: Luc Desaulniers (minardi).

I concur with Honda and the Prelude – it's such a nice looking coupe.

It has been revealed that but, for my obsession of the year, I have to say American Motors. I bought an Eagle this year and my deep dive into all things AMC has earned them very much respect in my eyes.

Over 70,000 km by Plane a Year: Travel Influencers Are Blowing Their Carbon Budgets and encouraging Europeans to Do the Same

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, travel influencers have a disproportionate climate footprint, generating an average of 10.0t of CO₂e emissions each just from flights in 2025, according to a new report by T3 Transportation Think Tank, commissioned by T&E.
  • It has been revealed that the study tracks 25 primarily European and US travel influencers representing millions of followers, and examines their role in the advertising strategy of airlines.
  • Sources indicate that the study shows that influencers predominantly take long-haul flights (49%) over medium (24%) and short-haul (27%) journeys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, travel influencers have a disproportionate climate footprint, generating an average of 10.0t of CO₂e emissions each just from flights in 2025, according to a new report by T3 Transportation Think Tank, commissioned by T&E. This is 16.7 times higher than the average European’s four leisure round trips and around 0.6 t CO₂e per tourist each year across all modes of transport for the 95% of their trips taking place in the EU. This does not yet include the travel emissions of the people they influenced.

It has been revealed that the study tracks 25 primarily European and US travel influencers representing millions of followers, and examines their role in the advertising strategy of airlines. Influencers took an average of 16 flights per year, visiting four times as many destinations as a standard European.

Sources indicate that the study shows that influencers predominantly take long-haul flights (49%) over medium (24%) and short-haul (27%) journeys. Long-haul flying is the most polluting form of transport: an economy long-haul flight generates roughly three to four times more emissions than a short-haul flight.

In total, these influencers flew a total distance of 1.8 million kilometers in 2025, equivalent to approximately 45 trips around the globe. Individually, each influencer flew an average of 72,244 km, equivalent to 34 return holiday flights between Paris and Athens.

Travel influencers are frequent flyers, with a disproportionate climate footprint. They regularly post about luxury, comfort and aspirational destinations. Influencers play a significant role in shaping where people choose to travel, thereby driving demand for high polluting flying. Through travel influencers, frequent air travel is normalised and encouraged.

Industry observers note that the study indicates that European and Middle Eastern airlines are ranked among the top 30 carriers that advertise on social media and websites. These include easyJet, Emirates and KLM. Even though airlines are not presently obliged to disclose their advertising budgets, the analysis reveals that social media, including influencer marketing, likely accounts for the largest marketing expenditure, around one third, with the UK seeing the highest spend (€50.2 million).

The list is dominated by airlines headquartered in the respective country and those that hold the most slots at the major international airports in each country. For example Air France spends more on social media advertisements in France (€2 million) compared to Spain (€29,000). Other carriers spending a lot on social media are easyJet and Aer Lingus, spending almost €26 million and around €7 million respectively. EasyJet spends more than twice on social media and online advertising than the following airlines.

Sources indicate that “Airlines have found a ridiculously cheap way of promoting climate intensive behaviour. They pay influencers to make very frequent and polluting long distance flights look normal and desirable. The average of 72,244 km shouldn’t be something to brag about… that would take an average European nearly 23 years to match” remarked Aiza Rodrigues Akhtar, T&E Aviation Campaigner. “The EU must enforce disclosure of airline-funded influencer promotions of harmful high-emission flights and enforce accountability of both parties.”.

Recent findings suggest that for airlines, partnering with travel influencers is remarkably cost-effective: it can cost just a few thousand euros¹ or just a free seat upgrade, yet it leads to significant results. Compared to traditional channels such as TV broadcasts or billboard displays, social media ads have a higher return on investment: posts that are liked, shared or reposted remain in the digital space for longer, significantly boosting visibility.

Yet, both influencers and airlines are not fully transparent when it comes to advertising. Influencers do not always clearly label their promotional content, and airlines do not publicly disclose how much they spend on digital advertising. Consumer organisations underline that any commercial promotion on social media should be clearly labelled so that consumers know what they are being marketed to and when. The EU Digital Fairness Act, currently under development, is key to tackling misleading influencer marketing and closing transparency loopholes. As travel influencers promote high-emission flights, any paid promotions must be clearly labelled as such.

Industry observers note that “Transparency is a first step, but it is not enough to prevent the damage caused by influencer ads for flying”, notes Rémi ter Haar, legal campaigner at Fossil Free Advertising. “Calling for more truthful advertising in the aviation sector is like playing a game of ‘whack-a-mole’. We must get ahead in the game and ban their advertising, for the sake of the climate and public health. We cannot expect people to behave more sustainably, only to then manipulate them through advertising into doing exactly the opposite.”.

According to recent reports, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) recognises that regulating advertising is key to changing the behaviours needed to limit global warming to 1.5°C. Marketing portrays luxury goods as necessities, and the IPCC cites long-distance holiday ads as an example of how the industry creates and normalises carbon-intensive desires. While the EU Audiovisual Media Services Directive prohibits promotions that encourage behavior harmful to the environment, this rule is often interpreted too narrowly. Airline advertising, which promotes carbon-intensive behaviour, should be included in its definition.

In a recent development, ¹ Influencers get paid between €269 to €2,692 for their travel content by airlines depending on the format: a 24-hour post (story), a static post or a short video (reel). Read more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Malin Akerman has a private disco in her upcoming Connecticut home, complete with a mixing deck and a smoke machine.

But ask the star of “The Hunting Wives” where she’s happiest in the house, and she’ll point you to a piece of living room furniture.

“Plopping down on our massive pink couch in the living room with my family,” the actress told The Wall Street Journal when he asked about her favorite spot.

It has been revealed that akerman, 48, moved to Connecticut in July with her husband, actor Jack Donnelly, and her son, Sebastian, 13. The family settled into a modern house built in 1988.

“The interior has an inviting flow, and all the rooms are cozy,” she noted.

Industry observers note that one room in particular gives her a good excuse to send out invitations. Alongside the DJ equipment, Akerman has a disco ball and a laser. “I love to DJ, dance and have friends over for parties,” she mentioned.

Anyone who ever danced at Akerman’s house in Los Angeles might recognize the decor. In May, when she listed her longtime Hollywood Hills home for $2.9 million, she told Elle Decor that her disco ball would be coming east.

In a recent development, she had a suggestion for whoever bought the place, too. “I sincerely hope the next owners put in a disco ball,” she said.

According to recent reports, akerman found that California home while working at a downtown L.A. restaurant. A regular learned she was looking for a rental and offered to show her a house he owned with his brother.

She spent three years there as a tenant before buying it in 2008. Over the years, she added a pool and turned the unfinished lower level into a primary suite that opened onto the garden, according to Elle Decor.

Staying at one address for two decades was a departure for Akerman. Her first home was a studio in Stockholm.

In a recent development, when she was 2, her father, Magnus, had job offers in Toronto and Newly introduced York. Her parents chose Canada, where the view from their townhouse gave their daughter something to do as she drifted off.

“At night, I fell asleep counting trains,” she told the Journal.

Her father returned to Sweden after her parents divorced. Akerman, then 6, stayed in Canada with her mother, Pia.

It has been revealed that at 12, she moved into a white house in Niagara-on-the-Lake, the Ontario town where her newly introduced stepfather had grown up. Two years later, the marriage ended. Her little brother, Marcus, went to live with his father. Akerman stayed with Pia.

“Given the friction, I don’t have many happy memories of the house,” she remarked.

Industry observers note that as she and her mother moved, Akerman changed schools. A drama elective she picked as a high school freshman gave her a circle of friends.

“Drama provided me with community and stability,” she recalled.

In a recent development, when a manager later encouraged her to move to Los Angeles, her best friend, Laura, went with her. A friend from high school took them in.

Acting work was slow to materialize, but Akerman studied the craft, and a role opposite Lisa Kudrow in “The Comeback” helped launch her career.

Now it’s Sebastian who has a role to celebrate at home. Akerman revealed that her son landed a part in Hulu’s “Paradise” on his first audition.

As for how quickly he might follow his mother into the family business, she kept her answer brief. “We’re taking it slow.”.

Sources indicate that akerman dates her turning point to her early 20s, when she began to feel confident with her longtime girlfriends in her corner. As she put it, “They made me feel more connected and provided emotional support.”.

Akerman will also soon be celebrating the season 2 premiere of "The Hunting Wives," which airs on Nov. 26.
